title: Mixtures and separation methods
summary: Learn the types of mixtures and the ways to separate them.
cards.0.p: In a mixture, two or more substances come together without bonding. The components keep their properties, their ratio can vary, and the mixture has no formula. The boiling point of a mixture is usually not constant either.
cards.0.key: A liquid whose temperature rises while it boils is not pure. It is a mixture. Salt water boiling at 1 atm is an example.
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: Salt and water mix without bonding, and their ratio can vary.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Water is a compound formed by H and O bonding together.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: Iron is an element made of one kind of atom.
cards.1.p: A mixture that is the same everywhere is called a homogeneous mixture or a solution. Usually the substance present in the larger amount is the solvent, and the substance spread through it is the solute. Air is a gaseous solution, and brass is a solid solution.
cards.1.key: An alloy is not a compound but a homogeneous mixture. The ratio of its components can vary.
cards.1.once.soru: What is brass (an alloy of copper and zinc)?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: In an alloy the metals are spread in the same ratio everywhere, and this ratio can vary.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: The components do not bond to form a new substance, and their ratio is not fixed.
cards.2.p: By the rule you just saw, like dissolves like. Polar water dissolves ionic salt and polar sugar. Nonpolar CCl4 dissolves nonpolar iodine.
cards.2.key: Dissolving is the solute particles spreading out among the solvent particles. In water, water molecules surround these particles, which is called hydration. Dissolving is a physical process.
cards.3.p: In a heterogeneous mixture the components are not spread evenly. A solid in a liquid is a suspension (muddy water). Two liquids that do not dissolve in each other form an emulsion (mayonnaise). A liquid or solid in a gas is an aerosol (fog, smoke).
cards.3.etk.soru: Sort each heterogeneous mixture by its type.
cards.3.etk.ogeler.1.2: Coffee grounds do not dissolve in the liquid and settle to the bottom when left to stand.
cards.3.etk.ogeler.4.2: With the help of egg yolk, oil is spread through water as droplets.
cards.3.etk.ogeler.6.2: It is solid particles spread through a gas.
cards.3.key: A suspension settles to the bottom when left to stand. An emulsion separates into layers over time. The egg yolk in mayonnaise slows this separation.
cards.3.once.soru: Which mixture forms when you shake olive oil and water?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: It is a mixture of two liquids that do not dissolve in each other.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: A suspension is a solid that does not dissolve in a liquid.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: Oil does not dissolve in water, so the mixture is not homogeneous.
cards.4.p: In a colloid the particles are bigger than in a solution but smaller than in a suspension. A colloid does not settle, but it scatters light, which is called the Tyndall effect. Milk and mayonnaise are colloidal emulsions.
cards.4.key: Colloid particles are about 1-1000 nm in size. Fog and smoke are colloidal aerosols. Headlights looking like beams in fog is also the Tyndall effect.
cards.5.p: Sieving separates coarse and fine solids such as sand and gravel. Filtering holds back solids that do not dissolve in a liquid, as in sandy water. In dialysis a membrane lets small particles through and holds back big ones.
cards.5.svg#4: the membrane lets small ones through,
cards.5.key: In kidney failure, blood is cleaned by dialysis. All three methods rely on differences in particle size.
cards.5.once.soru: What happens if you pour salt water through filter paper?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.yazi: The salt passes through with the water
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: Dissolved salt particles are very small. Filter paper cannot hold them back.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.yazi: The salt stays on the paper
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: Filtering only holds back undissolved solids.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.yazi: The water stays on the paper
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: Water passes through the paper easily.
cards.6.p: Iron, nickel and cobalt are attracted by a magnet, so iron filings and sulfur can be separated with a magnet. Flotation relies on differences in density. When water is added to sand mixed with sawdust, the sawdust floats and the sand sinks.
cards.6.etk.soru: Match each mixture with the best way to separate it.
cards.6.key: In flotation the liquid must not dissolve the components, and its density must be between theirs.
cards.7.p: Liquids that do not dissolve in each other form layers in a separatory funnel, and the denser one is drained from the bottom. A centrifuge spins the sample to collect dense particles at the bottom. In decanting, the liquid above a sediment is poured off.
cards.7.key: A separatory funnel cannot separate alcohol and water. A centrifuge separates blood cells from plasma and cream from milk.
cards.8.p: In extraction, one component is pulled out of a mixture with a solvent that dissolves it well. Brewing tea is an example. In crystallization, a hot saturated solution is cooled, and the extra solid separates out as pure crystals.
cards.8.key: Solids whose solubility changes differently with temperature are separated by fractional crystallization. To separate salt and sand, the mixture is put in water, filtered, and the filtrate is evaporated.
cards.9.p: Simple distillation separates components whose boiling points are very different. When salt water is heated, the water boils. The vapor condenses in the condenser and drips into the collecting flask, while the salt stays in the flask.
cards.9.key: In evaporation the water is lost. If you also want the water back, you need distillation.
cards.10.p: A fractional distillation column separates liquids with close boiling points. In a refinery, the volatile parts of crude oil such as gasoline collect at the top, and diesel and asphalt at the bottom.
cards.10.key: The substance with the lowest boiling point comes out of the top of the column. Liquid air is separated the same way. Nitrogen evaporates first, then oxygen.
cards.10.once.soru: In a refinery's distillation column, which collects at the very top?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: The one with the lowest boiling point rises highest.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: Asphalt has a very high boiling point, so it stays at the bottom.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: Diesel boils at a higher temperature than gasoline and collects lower down.
cards.11.p: In evaporation, the solvent escapes and the solid is left behind. This is how salt is made from seawater in salt pans. In sublimation, iodine or naphthalene turns into gas when heated and becomes solid again on a cold surface.
cards.11.key: In evaporation the solvent is lost. If you also want the water back, you need distillation.
cards.11.once.soru: What happens when you heat a mixture of iodine and sand?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: Iodine goes straight from solid to gas, and the vapor becomes solid again on a cold surface. The sand stays in the dish.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: Sand has a very high melting point.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: Sand does not sublime, and it stays in the dish when heated.
cards.12.p: In chromatography, a mixture is carried by a solvent (the mobile phase) across a stationary phase such as paper. The component that clings least to the stationary phase travels farthest. This is how ink dyes are separated.
cards.12.svg#5: The ink separates into its colors.
cards.12.key: Substances clinging to a surface is called adsorption. Chromatography is ideal for small amounts of mixtures, such as leaf pigments and doping tests.
cards.12.once.soru: A black marker spot rises on wet paper and separates into colors. Why?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: A dye that clings less to the paper is carried farther by the solvent.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: The separation happens on the paper, and there is no evaporation.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: The dyes stay the same. They only separate from each other.
cards.13.p:
• In a mixture the components keep their properties. Their ratio varies, and the boiling point is not constant.
• A solution has one phase. Suspensions, emulsions and aerosols are heterogeneous.
• Like dissolves like, and colloids show the Tyndall effect.
• Every separation method relies on a difference in some property, such as size, density, solubility or boiling point.
quiz.0.q: Match each mixture with the method used to separate it.
quiz.0.e: Salt dissolves in water, but sand does not. After filtering, the sand stays behind, and when the filtrate evaporates, the salt is left. Alcohol and water separate by boiling point, blood by density and iodine by subliming. Pigments separate by clinging differently to the stationary phase.
quiz.1.q: Sort each mixture by its type.
quiz.1.e: Sugar water, salt water and the alloy bronze are homogeneous mixtures, so they are solutions. In muddy water and coffee with grounds, the undissolved solid settles to the bottom, so they are suspensions. Olive oil and water, and mayonnaise, are made of two liquids that do not dissolve in each other, so they are emulsions.
quiz.2.q: At 60 °C at most 110 g of KNO₃ dissolves in 100 g of water, and at 20 °C at most 32 g. A saturated KNO₃ solution made with 150 g of water at 60 °C is cooled to 20 °C. How many grams of KNO₃ crystallize?
quiz.2.e: 150 g of water can dissolve 165 g of KNO₃ at 60 °C and 48 g at 20 °C. So 165 − 48 = 117 g of KNO₃ crystallizes out. The mass that comes out is proportional to the mass of water.
quiz.3.q: You have two clear liquids: one is sugar water, the other is very dilute gelatin. What is the easiest way to tell which one is a colloid?
quiz.3.o.0: Shine a flashlight from the side in the dark and look for the light's path
quiz.3.o.2: Leave it for a day and wait for it to settle
quiz.3.e: Colloid particles scatter light, and the path of the beam becomes visible. This is called the Tyndall effect, and it does not happen in sugar water. A colloid passes through a filter and does not settle. So filtering and waiting do not tell the two liquids apart.
quiz.3.y.1: Colloid particles also pass through the pores of filter paper. Both liquids filter the same way.
quiz.3.y.2: A colloid does not settle. After waiting, both liquids look the same.
quiz.3.y.3: A magnet only attracts substances such as iron, nickel and cobalt. It does not show particle size.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Find the colloid with light, dissolve salt and choose a separation method.
A:adimlar.0.metin: In a solution the dispersed particles are very small. In a colloid they are bigger (about 1-1000 nm), but they still do not settle. We will shine light into two glasses from the side.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: In which glass is the path of the light beam visible?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The ions in a solution are too small to scatter light.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: One liquid is a solution and the other a colloid. Their particle sizes are different.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The colloid particles in milk scatter light, and the beam's path becomes visible. This is called the Tyndall effect.
A:adimlar.1.metin: Water is a polar liquid, and gasoline is nonpolar. Olive oil is nonpolar too.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: We shake both tubes. In which one does the olive oil dissolve?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Polar water does not dissolve nonpolar oil.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Nonpolar gasoline dissolves nonpolar oil, forming a single-phase solution. In water, shaking spreads the oil as droplets, forming an emulsion. After waiting, the droplets join and form a layer on top.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Oil is not like polar water.
A:adimlar.2.metin: The largest mass of a substance that can dissolve in 100 g of water is called its solubility, and it changes with temperature. The container holds 100 g of water and 60 g of KNO₃. Heat the water and dissolve all the KNO₃.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: At around 38 °C, all 60 g of KNO₃ dissolves. A solution that has dissolved as much as it can is called a saturated solution. If you cool this solution, its solubility drops and the extra comes out as crystals. This is called crystallization.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Now 100 g of KNO₃ and 30 g of NaCl are dissolved in 100 g of hot water. Cool the solution to 20 °C and see what settles to the bottom.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: What settles to the bottom at 20 °C?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The solubility of NaCl barely changes with temperature. Look at the curves.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The solubility of NaCl is still 36 g at 20 °C. All 30 g stays dissolved.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The solubility of KNO₃ drops to 31.6 g at 20 °C, and about 68 g crystallizes. The solubility of NaCl barely changes, and all of it stays in solution. This method is called fractional crystallization.
A:adimlar.4.metin: To separate a mixture, you use a property in which its components differ. Choose the method that separates iron filings from sulfur powder, and play it.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: Iron is attracted by a magnet, and sulfur is not. Magnetic separation relies on this difference, and steel is sorted this way at scrapyards too. Nickel and cobalt are also attracted by magnets.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Olive oil and water do not dissolve in each other and separate into two layers. Choose the method that separates them, and play it.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: In a separatory funnel, the denser water collects at the bottom. When the tap is opened, the water drains first and the oil stays in the funnel. This method is used only for liquids that do not dissolve in each other. Alcohol and water cannot be separated this way.
A:adimlar.6.metin: You want to get back both the salt and the water from salt water. Choose the method that gives you both, and play it.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.tamam: In distillation the water boils, the vapor condenses in the condenser, and pure water drips into the collecting flask. The salt stays in the flask. If you only evaporated it, you would get the salt, but the water would escape into the air. For liquids with close boiling points, fractional distillation is used.
A:kapanis.0: In a mixture the components keep their properties. Their ratio can vary, and there is no definite boiling point.
A:kapanis.1: A homogeneous mixture, or solution, has one phase. A colloid scatters light and shows the Tyndall effect, while a solution does not.
A:kapanis.2: Like dissolves like. Polar water dissolves salt and sugar, and nonpolar gasoline dissolves oil.
A:kapanis.3: Solubility changes with temperature. When a saturated solution is cooled, the extra substance crystallizes.
A:kapanis.4: Every separation method relies on a difference in some property, such as magnetism, density, particle size or boiling point.
